actions.text:
There are two stretches here, and each one opens up one end of the range.

Step 1, odds: p/(1-p) compares "happens" to "doesn't happen", so it's a different number from p itself. At p = 0.5 the odds are 1. At p = 0.8 they're 4. At p = 0.99 they're 99, and as p gets close to 1 the odds grow without limit. So odds cover (0, ∞).

Step 2, log: the log turns (0, ∞) into the whole number line. log(1) = 0, log(4) ≈ +1.39, log(0.25) ≈ −1.39. As the odds shrink towards 0, the log falls towards −∞.

So p = 0.5 lands on 0, and 0.2 and 0.8 land at the same distance on either side of it.
In your own words: what happens to the log-odds when p gets very close to 0, and why?

actions.text: In a sorted list, the middle item splits the list into two sides you can predict: everything to its left is smaller or equal, and everything to its right is larger or equal. Take [3, 8, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40] and look for 31. The middle is 19. Since 31 > 19, and every item left of 19 is even smaller, 31 can't be on the left, so you drop 3, 8, 12 and 19 without looking at them. Now shuffle the list to [25, 3, 40, 19, 8, 31, 12]. The middle is still 19, but 31 could be on either side, so that one comparison rules nothing out.
Try it on the sorted list [2, 5, 9, 14, 20, 27, 33] while looking for 5. You compare 5 with the middle item, 14. Which items can you now drop, and how do you know 5 isn't among them?

ancien-regime.label: The Ancien Régime and its crisis

ancien-regime/fiscal-crisis.statement: Royal debt and an unequal tax system, where the privileged estates paid little, pushed the monarchy to call for reform.
ancien-regime/fiscal-crisis.drawn: France's debt after funding the American War of Independence
ideas: privileged estates exempt from most taxes
failed reforms forced the king to seek new consent

misconceptions.check: Treats the revolution as caused only by peasant hunger, ignoring the fiscal and political crisis

ancien-regime/estates-inequality.statement: Society was divided into three legally unequal estates, and the Third Estate bore most of the burden despite being the vast majority.
ancien-regime/estates-inequality.drawn: voting by estate in the Estates-General of 1789

misconceptions.check: Thinks the Third Estate was uniformly poor peasants, not including the bourgeoisie

revolution-outbreak/national-assembly.statement: The Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, claiming sovereignty for the nation rather than the king.
revolution-outbreak/national-assembly.drawn: the Tennis Court Oath of June 1789

misconceptions.check: Thinks the monarchy was abolished in 1789

revolution-outbreak/popular-action.statement: Popular uprisings in Paris and the countryside made the political change irreversible.

misconceptions.check: Believes the Bastille mattered because many prisoners were freed

radicalization/terror-dynamics.statement: War, internal revolt and fear of counter-revolution pushed leaders toward emergency rule and the Terror.
radicalization/terror-dynamics.drawn: the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre

misconceptions.check: Explains the Terror as only one man's cruelty with no wartime pressure

napoleon-legacy/rise-and-legacy.statement: Instability let a general seize power, keeping some revolutionary gains like legal equality while ending the republic.
napoleon-legacy/rise-and-legacy.drawn: Napoleon's 1799 coup and the Civil Code

misconceptions.check: Thinks Napoleon restored the Ancien Régime

probes.prompt: In the Estates-General of 1789, each estate had one vote. Why did the Third Estate object?

options.label: It was the vast majority but could be outvoted by the other two estates
It was made up only of poor peasants
It wanted the king to have no role at all

probes.prompt: A government is deeply in debt, its richest groups pay little tax, and bread prices spike. Based on France in 1789, what is most likely?

options.label: Hunger alone causes revolt; politics and finance don't matter
Fiscal crisis forces calls for reform, and popular unrest then makes change hard to reverse
The privileged groups voluntarily give up their exemptions

probes.prompt: Why do revolutions sometimes turn to emergency rule and violence against suspected enemies? Use what you know about France in 1793-94, or reason it out.
